text: Sir John Bramston, GCMG, CB (14 November 1832 – 13 September 1921), was a politician in Queensland (now part of Australia) and a British colonial government administrator in Queensland and Hong Kong. He served as Assistant Under-Secretary of State for the Colonies in London for more than 20 years, retiring in 1898 and being created Knight Commander of the Order of St Michael and St George (KCMG) upon retirement. Born on 14 November 1832 in Roxwell, Essex, Bramston was the second son of Thomas William Bramston (later MP for South Essex) of Skreens, Essex, and his wife Eliza, daughter of Admiral Sir Eliab Harvey. He was educated at Winchester College and Balliol College, Oxford, where he graduated with a B.A. in 1854, became Fellow of All Souls College, Oxford the following year, and earned a D.C.L. in 1863. He entered the Middle Temple in November 1854 and was called to the bar in June 1857. He went to Queensland in 1859 as private secretary to Sir George Bowen, the first Governor of Queensland, holding that post for two years before resigning. On 3 July 1863, he was appointed a Member of the Queensland Legislative Council and served in the first Ministry formed by his friend Sir Robert Herbert, the first Premier of Queensland, from July 1863 to February 1866, acting briefly as Attorney-General from 31 August 1865 to 11 September 1865. Although his membership of the Legislative Council was lifetime, he resigned on 17 November 1869. Robert Herbert established a farm in the Brisbane area and lived there with Bramston, who named their house Herston, a combination of their surnames, which later became the name of the suburb of Herston. Bramston returned to England, where he remained for two years, acting as Assistant Boundary Commissioner for Devon and Cornwall under the Reform Act of 1867. He returned to Queensland in 1868 and was elected in the by-election on 3 April 1871 following Charles Haley's resignation as Member of the Queensland Legislative Assembly for Burnett, holding the seat until 8 December 1873, when the electorate was abolished in a redistribution. During this time, he served as Queensland's Attorney-General in the Palmer Ministry from 3 May 1870 to 2 January 1874. On 12 December 1872 at St John's Cathedral in Brisbane, Bramston married Eliza Isabella Russell, daughter of Rev. Harry Vane Russell and niece of the Governor of Queensland, George Phipps, 2nd Marquess of Normanby (who had married Laura Russell, sister to Harry Russell), with the service conducted by Bishop Edward Tufnell. The Governor hosted a wedding reception at Government House, and the couple honeymooned in Sydney and Tasmania. In 1874, Bramston was appointed Attorney General of Hong Kong, replacing Julian Pauncefote, and at times acted as a judge in Hong Kong. In June 1876, he was appointed Assistant Under-Secretary of State in the Colonial Office, serving on a mission to Berlin in connection with the Angra Pequena negotiations in July 1886, in which year he was created Companion of the Order of the Bath. In October 1887, Bramston's death was announced in the Queensland newspapers, leading to the publication of many obituaries, but it was later revealed to be an error due to a misinterpretation of a telegram. In 1892, he was appointed Registrar of the Order of St. Michael and St. George. In 1899, he was sent as Royal Commissioner alongside Admiral Sir James Erskine to inquire into French treaty rights in Newfoundland, a dispute settled by the Entente Cordiale of 1904; he was also a member of the Royal Commission for the Paris Exhibition of 1900. In the 1900 New Year Honours list, he was promoted to Knight Grand Cross of the Order of St Michael and St George (GCMG), and received the order from Queen Victoria during an investiture at Windsor Castle on 1 March 1900. His wife, Lady Bramston, died in 1920. Bramston died at Wimbledon on Tuesday 13 September 1921 and was buried at the Wimbledon Cemetery.
